title: Plant-Based Diets
summary: Josh and Chuck (with the show's iHeart intro voice, who co-hosts this episode as Chuck) explore plant-based diets: the spectrum of plant-based eating types (vegan, vegetarian, lacto-ovo, pescatarian, flexitarian), historical and modern meat consumption by country and region, religious diet rules (kosher, halal, Jainism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Ethiopian Orthodox fasting, Seventh-day Adventists), practical tips for eating more plants, health pros and cons including B12, bone fractures, stroke and cancer risk, motivations like animal welfare and mindful eating, and environmental impact including greenhouse gas emissions, water use, and deforestation. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about blacksmithing.

segments.title: Opening banter and defining plant-based diets
segments.summary: The hosts joke about starting late and whether anyone eats plants, then begin defining plant-based diets as an umbrella term that includes vegan, vegetarian, lacto-ovo, and pescatarian eating.

segments.title: Vegetarian variations and US meat consumption
segments.summary: Further discussion of vegetarian subtypes such as ovo and lacto-ovo, with a note that vegans avoid honey and all animal products. The hosts cite US per capita meat consumption figures of roughly 123 to 150 kilograms.

segments.title: Historical diets in Ireland and the colonies
segments.summary: Historically plant-based diets were the default for many people, such as potato-heavy diets in pre-famine Ireland. Meat was tied to elite status, and colonial America ate more meat than England because of abundant land.

segments.title: Mediterranean diet history and rising meat consumption with prosperity
segments.summary: Italy's traditional diet was largely plant-based and Mediterranean before meat consumption rose after World War Two. Meat consumption tends to rise with national prosperity. In nineteenth-century America, officials encouraged meat eating, including during an 1832 cholera outbreak.

segments.title: Meat consumption across Africa and Asia
segments.summary: Per capita meat consumption varies widely across African countries, from about 65 kilograms in South Africa to about 4 kilograms in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Statistics are inconsistent. Asian countries eat less meat than the US, and India and Taiwan rank high for vegetarianism.

segments.title: Southeast Asia, India and per capita meat numbers
segments.summary: Several Southeast Asian countries have very low per capita meat consumption. India has the highest share of vegetarians, around 38 to 40 percent, and eats about 6.6 kilograms of meat per capita.

segments.title: Religious diet rules: kosher, halal, Israel, Ethiopian Orthodox, Adventists
segments.summary: Religious dietary laws affect meat eating. Kosher and halal rules restrict animals and slaughter methods, which can lead adherents toward vegetarianism. Israel ranks second for vegetarianism. Ethiopian Orthodox fast days mean many followers are mostly vegetarian. About 36 percent of Seventh-day Adventists are lacto-ovo vegetarian.

segments.title: Buddhism, Japan's meat ban, and Hinduism
segments.summary: Buddhism links vegetarianism to nonviolence. Japan effectively banned meat from 675 to 1872 under Buddhist and Confucian influence. Around 80 percent of Hindus eat a plant-based diet, and in India vegetarianism is tied to social status. Hindu nationalist enforcement has included beatings and at least one lynching over meat, especially beef.

segments.title: Jainism and Sikhism vegetarianism
segments.summary: About 92 percent of Jains and 59 percent of Sikhs in India are vegetarian. Jains are described as avoiding harm to living beings, including dusting seats.

segments.title: Practical tips for eating more plants
segments.summary: Harvard Health advice includes filling half the plate with vegetables of varied colors, treating meat as a side rather than the centerpiece, using the Zimbabwe hand jive portion guide from Dr. Kazim Mauji (1993), choosing healthier fats, cooking one vegetarian meal a week, and whole grains.

segments.title: Fruit for dessert, greens, and sleep
segments.summary: The hosts discuss swapping dessert for fruit or a small piece of dark chocolate, eating more salads and leafy greens, and a joking tip about early bedtime and breakfast.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the next section on motivations for vegetarianism.

segments.title: Reasons people go plant-based: health, nutrition, animal welfare, ethics
segments.summary: People adopt plant-based diets for health and weight, intuitively viewing plants as healthier. Legumes offer protein, fiber and no cholesterol. There are roughly twenty thousand legume species, including neglected and underutilized legumes (NUL). Factory farming and animal welfare are major motivations. Ethical vegans question whether eating meat is normal, a concept called carnism.

segments.title: Mindful eating
segments.summary: Mindful eating, meaning deliberate awareness of food and its effects on health, the world and animals, is another reason people move to plant-based diets. The hosts tie it to religious diets.

segments.title: Ultra-processed vegan food and the Mediterranean diet
segments.summary: Vegan eating can be unhealthy if built on processed foods, sugar, or fries. Whole foods are recommended. Studies link the Mediterranean diet to lower rates of some cancers, diabetes, cognitive decline and cardiovascular disease.

segments.title: Protein, vitamin B12 deficiency, and bone fractures
segments.summary: Vegans are most likely to have inadequate protein intake. About 52 percent of vegans and 7 percent of vegetarians are B12 deficient, versus under 1 percent of meat eaters. Vegetarians have a 25 percent higher hip fracture risk and vegans 131 percent higher, controlling for BMI. Hosts discuss possible reasons, including B12 and muscle mass.

segments.title: Cancer, stroke and all-cause mortality findings
segments.summary: Vegetarians and vegans have a 10 to 18 percent lower cancer risk than meat eaters. All-cause mortality was not different between groups. Vegetarians had a 20 percent higher risk of hemorrhagic stroke in a 2021 analysis of a British cohort of about 65,000 people, with vegan stroke risk not determined.

segments.title: Environmental impact of meat: emissions, water, deforestation
segments.summary: Meat production has a larger carbon footprint than most plant foods. A 2019 Sustainability study found vegetarians have 33 percent lower emissions and vegans 53 percent lower. Beef has the highest emissions and water footprint; chocolate and almonds exceed beef in water use. Beef drives about 40 percent of tropical deforestation, and livestock may account for a fifth to a quarter of human water use. Livestock also carries zoonotic disease risk.

segments.title: Hosts reflect on personal diet changes
segments.summary: The hosts say they eat more vegetables and less red meat, with Josh joking about his quarter pounders. The transition to listener mail follows.

segments.title: Listener mail: blacksmithing
segments.summary: Listener Tate Avent writes that a blacksmithing episode four years ago sparked his lasting hobby, and shares photos of his work.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Josh invites listeners to send similar stories to the show's email address, and the iHeart announcer closes the episode.
